summary: The machine has the key pieces to start building the Node.js Mongoose ATM monitor against the provided Azure DocumentDB cluster: Node.js, npm/npx, Docker, the documentdb MCP server, Microsoft Learn search, and a broad set of documentdb-* agent skills. Most cold answers the model gave were recoverable (some were outright wrong or described the older Cosmos DB/Mongo API). Missing items that would materially speed development or manual verification are mongosh and the DocumentDB Agent Kit; several cold-answer facts must be corrected in the sample documentation or agent kit before coding proceeds to avoid mis-provisioning or wrong connection handling.
summary_points: All essential runtime tools for building the Node.js sample are present: node (v24), npm/npx, Docker, and az (signed-in).

The documentdb MCP server is available and can inspect and verify the live cluster; many DocumentDB-specific skills are installed (connection, driver, indexing, vector search, local-deployment, etc.).

Several cold answers from memory confuse Cosmos DB (RU-based Mongo API / older hostnames/ports) with the current Azure DocumentDB (vCore / mongoClusters); these must be corrected before the build to avoid wrong connection strings, CLI commands, or provisioning choices.
Missing accelerators that would speed the build: the DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx install) and the mongosh CLI for manual checks; workarounds exist but add friction.
No blocking missing tool prevents starting development; the build can proceed with workarounds, so verdict is ready_with_gaps.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run, test and build the Node.js + Mongoose ATM monitor sample (npm install, npm start, npx tasks).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run Node.js sample or install packages.
tools.workaround: Install an appropriate Node.js version (>=24) via nvm; not needed here since present.

tools.name: npx / npm
tools.needed_for: Install project deps, run sample scripts and (if desired) add skills via npx.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot bootstrap packages or install skill accelerators via npx.
tools.workaround: Install npm/npx through Node.js distribution; not required here.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional local DocumentDB gateway container for local dev/tests; can also run other test containers.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the local Gateway container for integration tests; must test against live cluster only.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and run unit tests with mongodb-memory-server or mocks; or install Docker.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources (optionally verify cluster resource, firewall rules, roles) and to read connection strings or resource metadata if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to inspect control-plane resource metadata; cannot call az commands locally to look up connection outputs.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server or the Azure portal to inspect cluster configuration.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection and verification: list databases/collections, sample documents, create/list indexes, run aggregates and explain plans against the live cluster.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present and responding with 18 data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, aggregate, etc.)
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent cannot programmatically verify what the app created on the live cluster or run explain() to validate indexes.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh or Azure portal to inspect cluster, but documentdb MCP tooling is strongly preferred.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn documentation search)
tools.needed_for: Ground facts, verify current CLI/ARM/Bicep resource types, connection-string formats, vector/index docs and other authoritative guidance.
tools.detail: Microsoft Learn search and fetch tools available.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to verify up-to-date product docs and sample code; increased risk of outdated assumptions.
tools.workaround: Rely on installed skills' text or raw web browsing; but learn is present so use it.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance on configuring MongoDB clients for Azure DocumentDB (connection pools, timeouts, retries) and diagnosis of connection errors.
tools.impact_if_missing: Higher chance of connection misconfiguration (pool exhaustion, timeouts) in sample code.
tools.workaround: Follow general MongoDB driver best practices and documentdb-driver skill guidance.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver-level recommendations: singleton MongoClient, connection reuse across serverless/function processes, Mongoose integration patterns.
tools.impact_if_missing: Increased risk of incorrect client usage and connection leaks in the sample app.
tools.workaround: Follow standard Mongoose docs and common singleton patterns; but the skill is present and should be used.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative local development guidance: gateway image, local ports (10260), TLS and SCRAM settings, docker-compose for integration tests.
tools.detail: Installed skill; describes Gateway Docker image and port 10260 for Mongo wire protocol.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder may incorrectly choose the official mongo:latest image and port 27017, leading to mismatch with DocumentDB local gateway behavior.
tools.workaround: If not using the local gateway, test against the live cluster via DOCUMENTDB_URI per the skill_md; ideally install and use the gateway image.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-full-text-search (skills)
tools.needed_for: Designing vector and text indexes for the sample (embedding field, cosmosSearch options, index kinds: vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann and full-text search via createSearchIndexes / $search).
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of creating non-optimal or unsupported index types and wrong vector-query syntax.
tools.workaround: Consult Microsoft Learn docs (available via learn tool) for the exact index creation templates.

tools.name: documentdb-mcp-setup (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance on wiring the documentdb MCP server into an agentic client if the builder wants to automate profile setup/test harness integration.
tools.detail: Installed skill that helps configure CONNECTION_PROFILES and MCP auth.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent may struggle to programmatically connect to the MCP server; manual setup would be required.
tools.workaround: Manually configure the documentdb MCP connection profile as the run environment suggests; the skill helps but is not mandatory.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual verification: run ad-hoc queries, inspect indexes, test change-stream cursors by hand.
tools.impact_if_missing: Slows interactive debugging and manual verification steps; the documentdb MCP server mitigates this but some engineers prefer mongosh.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's data-plane tools to inspect documents, indexes and run explains; or install mongosh (`npm install -g mongosh` or download binary).

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

tools.name: azd, bicep, terraform
tools.needed_for: Infrastructure as code for cluster provisioning (not required for this sample run because provisioning is not allowed).
tools.impact_if_missing: Only relevant if the builder wanted to provision clusters from this machine; run policy forbids provisioning so not required.
tools.workaround: Use provided cluster; if IaC needed later, install azd/bicep/terraform per Microsoft docs.

tools.name: azure (MCP server)
tools.detail: Azure MCP server present with many control-plane tools.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient access to Azure control-plane docs and CLI generation, but not required for the sample run.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI or the Azure portal; the azure MCP server is available here as an accelerator.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — installed skills cover many areas but the named agent kit accelerator from the known list (DocumentDB Agent Kit) is not present; installing it with `npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit` would centrally provide design templates and code snippets that speed this sample's build.

mongosh (install via package or OS package manager) — not strictly an 'accelerator' listed in known_accelerators but present in the Known Tools list as useful; install with `npm install -g mongosh` or download the mongosh distribution to make interactive verification faster.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB accounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. The current resource type for the managed MongoDB (vCore) offering is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older Cosmos DB account resource model (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) used by the Cosmos DB 'MongoDB API' accounts. The newer vCore-managed MongoDB clusters are deployed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and are a different resource type.

confusion_sources.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos DB account docs — older Cosmos model)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the cold answer they might create or manage the wrong resource type (databaseAccounts) when attempting IaC or CLI operations, leading to failed deployments or operating against Cosmos DB RU-based accounts rather than the vCore mongoClusters the sample must use.
improvements: Update quickstarts and agent skill examples that mention resource type to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore-managed MongoDB clusters (Learn page: templates/microsoft.documentdb/mongoclusters).
Add a short note in the agent kit's 'provisioning' guidance explaining the two different product families (mongoClusters vCore vs Cosmos DB databaseAccounts with Mongo API).

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create ... (part of core az CLI).
confusions.grounded_answer: The command group for vCore-managed MongoDB clusters is exposed under az documentdb mongocluster (and az cosmosdb mongocluster in some CLI distributions), e.g., `az documentdb mongocluster create` / `az cosmosdb mongocluster create`. This is part of the DocumentDB/az extension command surface rather than the legacy az cosmosdb create command used for RU-based Cosmos DB accounts.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
az cosmosdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'create' flow (`az cosmosdb create`) manages RU-based Cosmos accounts; the vCore mongoClusters subcommands are newer and appear under documentdb/cosmosdb cli groups (preview/extension).

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (legacy Cosmos account create docs)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses az cosmosdb create they may end up provisioning or attempting to manage a RU-based Cosmos DB account rather than the vCore mongoClusters resource type; this would mismatch the sample's run environment (which already has a vCore mongo cluster).
improvements: Document the exact az CLI commands for creating a mongoClusters resource in the agent kit and quickstarts and show `az documentdb mongocluster create` as the canonical command for vCore clusters.
Add an explicit note in the 'provisioning' documentation warning that `az cosmosdb create` targets RU-based Cosmos DB accounts and is not the same as `mongocluster`.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (set kind to MongoDB). Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database/collection.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed offering use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource in Bicep/ARM (and corresponding azapi/AVM modules for Terraform). The older Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts resource is for RU-based Cosmos DB accounts (the Cosmos DB 'MongoDB API').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM/Terraform examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the legacy Cosmos DB ARM resource model; newer vCore clusters use the mongoClusters resource. The names are similar and both live under Microsoft.DocumentDB, which causes confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Terraform resource type results in incorrect IaC and inability to manage the exact cluster type the sample expects (the run environment's cluster is a mongoCluster).
improvements: Add a short Bicep/Terraform snippet to the agent kit that shows how to declare Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and point out the difference from databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) connection string example: mongodb://...@my-account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin. Port 10255 and replicaSet=globaldb are normally required.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) the recommended connection strings typically use SRV (mongodb+srv://<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/...) with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256; older Cosmos DB Mongo API examples (host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 with replicaSet=globaldb) are for the RU-based Cosmos accounts. Use the connection string returned by the cluster's portal/az output (store it in DOCUMENTDB_URI).

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (classic RU-based examples and port 10255)
Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (mongocluster SRV example)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (mongocluster SRV examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The classic Cosmos DB Mongo API used hostnames like *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com with port 10255 and replicaSet=globaldb; vCore/mongoClusters prefer cluster-level SRV hostnames under mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and may not use the 10255 pattern. The two offerings share 'MongoDB' in marketing and similar hostnames, causing the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB connection docs (10255 examples)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample hardcodes the 10255/replicaSet=globaldb pattern it may fail to connect to vCore mongoClusters (wrong host suffix, SRV vs A-records, or missing SCRAM/Azure AD options). This would cause authentication/connection errors at runtime.
improvements: In the sample README and templates, instruct builders to always use the DOCUMENTDB_URI provided by the cluster (from the portal/az output) and not to hardcode ports/options; show both SRV and URI examples for vCore mongoclusters.
Add a short agent-kit snippet that demonstrates how to parse and consume the SRV vs non-SRV connection strings and which driver options to set (tls=true, authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256).

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos billed by RUs; there is also a newer vCore/dedicated cluster offering for MongoDB-compatible workloads (dedicated compute tiers billed by vCores). Expect RU-based for classic Cosmos accounts and vCore-style for dedicated MongoDB-compatible clusters.
confusions.grounded_answer: There are two distinct models: RU-based Cosmos DB accounts (classic Cosmos Mongo API) are provisioned/billed by RUs; the vCore-managed offering (mongoClusters / Azure DocumentDB) is billed by compute (vCores/tiers such as M30) and storage. The sample's run environment (compute tier M30) uses vCore billing.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing: compute vCores and storage)
Convert vCores to RUs (explanatory docs showing both models)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both RU-based Cosmos DB accounts and vCore mongoClusters are in the Azure data platform and historically the Cosmos umbrella blurred the lines; the cold answer mixed both and lacked the decisive mapping to the vCore cluster the sample uses.
confusions.build_risk: Using RU-based provisioning logic or cost/throughput expectations would mis-size the sample's assumptions (e.g., expecting RU quotas, autoscale behavior) and could cause incorrect guidance in readmes or tests.
improvements: In the agent kit and quickstarts, explicitly call out the two pricing models and say which one each sample targets; for this sample, state 'this sample targets vCore mongoClusters (M30) and so you should think in vCores and storage'.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB drivers connect using SCRAM username/password derived from Cosmos account keys; direct Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication for MongoDB API is not generally available.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is supported as an allowed authentication mode (clusters accept NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID). Drivers can use SCRAM (native) credentials, and the service also supports Microsoft Entra ID based auth/config when enabled on the cluster.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create — --auth-allowed-modes shows MicrosoftEntraID support
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (Entra ID support noted)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer generalized from classic Cosmos DB behavior (where Azure AD for the Mongo API was historically limited) and missed that the vCore mongoClusters explicitly support Microsoft Entra ID authentication modes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Azure AD is unsupported, they may avoid implementing secure (Entra-backed) authentication and instead hardcode credentials or choose an insecure pattern for the sample.
improvements: Update the driver/connection guidance in documentdb-driver and the sample README to mention Microsoft Entra ID as an available authentication mode and show a short example or link to `az documentdb mongocluster` docs explaining enabling Entra ID.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (mongodb or Mongoose for Node). Do not use @azure/cosmos for MongoDB API workloads.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the official MongoDB drivers (or Mongoose for ODM patterns). The service exposes a MongoDB wire protocol; do not use @azure/cosmos for MongoDB API workloads. For vector/search features you still use the MongoDB aggregation `$search` / cosmosSearch operator as documented.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
Quickstart: Use MongoDB drivers (Node.js) with Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style knnVector (createIndex with knnVector) with indexType hnsw or ivf (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF families).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes and multiple index kinds: vector-ivf, vector-hnsw and vector-diskann (DiskANN), created via the service's createIndexes/createSearchIndexes templates using cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions (not the MongoDB 7 knnVector exact syntax). Querying is done with $search + cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index kinds and create examples)
Quickstart: Use vector search with Node.js in Azure DocumentDB (create index examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer repeated MongoDB 7+ knnVector syntax; Azure DocumentDB exposes its vector index creation via cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions or createIndexes templates with kind vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann. The concepts map (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) but the exact create syntax differs.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong createIndex syntax (knnVector) will fail on DocumentDB; the app must call the DocumentDB-specific create index command or the correct createIndexes payload to make vector indexes.
improvements: Add explicit code snippets in the agent kit showing how to call createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions to create vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann indexes.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes for basic full-text and integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for advanced/hybrid (text+vector) search because Atlas Search isn't available.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes built-in full-text and vector search capabilities: use createSearchIndexes / createIndexes with cosmosSearch options and query via the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch). Hybrid (lexical + vector) search is supported natively (cosine/L2/IP similarity combined with pre-filters) without an external Cognitive Search pipeline in many scenarios.

grounding_links.title: Vector search and $search (Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB)
Full-text search and hybrid search docs (cosmosSearch / $search)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the need for an external Azure Cognitive Search pipeline (common for Cosmos DB/NoSQL hybrid scenarios) and used MongoDB text indexes as default. The DocumentDB service integrates text + vector search natively via cosmosSearch, so external Cognitive Search is not required for the features the sample will use.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search integration guidance (for scenarios that still require it)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder errs toward externalizing search into Cognitive Search, the sample will be more complex and may not demonstrate the built-in $search + cosmosSearch hybrid capability that DocumentDB provides.
improvements: Document the native $search + cosmosSearch capabilities in the agent kit quickstarts and show a short example combining vector and text filters.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB Mongo API supports various versions up through newer ones depending on account; some admin commands and server-side JavaScript and some aggregation stages may not be supported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) explicitly supports MongoDB wire protocol/server versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (depending on cluster serverVersion selection). The service supports the vast majority of MongoDB operators (official compatibility docs list supported/unsupported operators); some administrative or server-level commands and a small subset of operators are not supported (see compatibility matrix).

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (supported versions and operator matrix)
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (wire protocol versions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged and conflated multiple offering versions (some Cosmos Mongo API accounts had earlier version caps). The current vCore product documents explicit support for modern wire versions and provides a compatibility matrix.
confusions.build_risk: If builder assumes unsupported aggregation stages or mismatched wire protocol, tests may fail or driver handshake errors may occur. The compatibility matrix must be consulted for any advanced feature used.
improvements: Add a single compatibility link and a short note in the sample README that points the developer to the 'compatibility-query-language' page for exact operator/aggregation coverage.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Run the official MongoDB server locally (mongo:7.0) on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development use the provided DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 and requires TLS + SCRAM-SHA-256 configuration for local development. The official mongo:latest image is a general fallback for generic Mongo behavior but does not emulate DocumentDB-specific features (vector search, cosmosSearch, auth modes, ports).

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell (gateway SRV examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the widely used practice of using the upstream MongoDB server for local dev; DocumentDB provides a Gateway image to emulate service-specific features and ports (10260), so the simple mongo:latest approach is insufficient for DocumentDB-specific tests.
confusions.build_risk: Using mongo:27017 for local tests would miss DocumentDB-specific behavior (vector indexes, cosmosSearch syntax, port/TLS differences), yielding tests that don't reproduce the live cluster behavior.
improvements: Document the Gateway image and port 10260 in the sample's local-development README and provide a docker-compose example using the Gateway image with TLS env vars.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are available when the account exposes a MongoDB server version that supports them (MongoDB 3.6+). Typically no extra account flag is needed for standard Cosmos MongoDB clusters; use collection.watch with fullDocument:'updateLookup'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB; for single-shard clusters and standard vCore clusters you can use the driver's watch API. For multi-shard clusters there is an opt-in feature for multi-shard change streams that must be enabled in the cluster Features (the portal provides a toggle). Change streams support resume tokens and historical replay (subject to retention limits).

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is broadly correct about basic support but omitted the important multi-shard enablement caveat and historical replay/resume token guidance.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes multishard change streams by default it may fail without the feature toggle enabled; the builder must handle resume tokens and implement a strategy for saving them.
improvements: Add a sentence to the sample README: 'Change streams are supported; for multi-shard clusters enable the "Change streams for multishard clusters" feature in the portal (or via CLI) before relying on cross-shard stream behavior.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service-specific MCP server would be 'documentdb' (documentdb MCP). The general Azure MCP server covers control-plane operations but not the documentdb data-plane inspection.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the machine inventory contains a working 'documentdb' MCP server that provides data-plane commands (list databases, create/list indexes, find/aggregate/explain). The 'azure' MCP server covers control-plane operations but is separate.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for Microsoft's JSON document database service; it was rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB 'MongoDB API' is an API surface on top of the Cosmos engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong/misleading: historically 'DocumentDB' was the original name (2014) that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; however the current 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' is the rebranded name for the vCore-managed MongoDB offering that used to be called 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'. It is distinct from the RU-based Cosmos DB Mongo API and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Several similarly named products and historical renames (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB, Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore → Azure DocumentDB) create overlapping terminology; the cold answer conflated historical naming with the modern vCore product.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB vs Azure DocumentDB naming pages

confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion could lead the builder to pick the wrong quickstart docs, create the wrong resource type, or use the wrong connection/port patterns.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Terminology' note in the agent kit and sample README that lists: (1) 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) = vCore mongoClusters', (2) 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) = RU-based Cosmo account with Mongo API', (3) 'Original Azure DocumentDB (2014) → Cosmos DB historically', and link to the FAQ.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the hood it's the Cosmos DB engine implementing a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol (not a stock mongod). Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers but expect differences in supported commands and semantics.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current vCore product (Azure DocumentDB) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) which is implemented on top of PostgreSQL; it exposes a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers and must consult the compatibility matrix, but the implementation is DocumentDB (not the Cosmos DB engine).

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer generalized from prior Cosmos DB messaging; the vCore product uses the DocumentDB engine (open-source) as the implementation, which matters for some operational semantics and compatibility notes.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the wrong underlying engine could cause incorrect assumptions about unsupported server-side extensions or licensing; however application-level MongoDB drivers remain valid.
improvements: Add a one-line engine note in README: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses the open-source DocumentDB engine (built on PostgreSQL) and exposes a MongoDB wire protocol — use standard Mongo drivers but consult compatibility pages for edge cases.'

confusions.question: Which database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_banking_16 for all collections and operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment and sample prompt explicitly mandate using the database named sample_banking_16.

grounding_links.title: sample prompt / skill_md (run environment database name)

confusions.question: What vector index definition does this sample rely on for ATM embedding search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a knnVector index on the embedding field using MongoDB 7 knnVector syntax with indexType 'hnsw'.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports vector indexes but the service uses its own createIndexes/createSearchIndexes payloads and cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions with kinds vector-ivf, vector-hnsw or vector-diskann (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF). The sample should create a vector index using the DocumentDB index API (kind: vector-hnsw or vector-diskann) rather than the MongoDB knnVector DDL syntax.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (index kinds and creation examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used upstream MongoDB's knnVector style DDL; DocumentDB implements vector indexes via the cosmosSearch index API with explicit 'kind' values.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create a knnVector index with upstream Mongo syntax on DocumentDB will fail; the sample must call the DocumentDB createIndexes/createSearchIndexes API.
improvements: Provide a ready-made createIndexes JSON snippet in the sample's seed/setup script that uses 'cosmosSearchOptions' with the desired kind and parameters (dimensions, similarity, m/efConstruction, or numLists) and reference the vector-search docs.

confusions.question: What collection names and basic schemas will the sample create?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections: atm_status, network_summary, alerts with example schemas.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a sensible sample design and aligns with the prompt (heartbeat docs, a single network_summary doc, and alerts collection). The builder should follow documentdb-data-modeling guidance for document sizes, indexing and embedding storage.

confusions.question: How will the sample open and use change streams to detect status changes?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the driver's watch API with a $match on updateDescription.updatedFields.status and fullDocument:'updateLookup', handle resume tokens.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use collection.watch(...) with an appropriate pipeline, fullDocument:'updateLookup' to get current document state on update events, and persist resume tokens for resumption. For cross-shard change streams, enable the cluster feature first.

confusions.question: How should the app read the cluster connection string and what mongoose options to use?
confusions.cold_answer: Read from DOCUMENTDB_URI; connect with mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser:true, useUnifiedTopology:true, ssl:true, replicaSet:'globaldb', retryWrites:false, authSource:'admin' });
confusions.grounded_answer: Always read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI (do not hardcode). Use modern Mongoose (7.x) defaults — many legacy options (useNewUrlParser, useUnifiedTopology) are no-ops in current drivers. Do not assume `replicaSet=globaldb` or port 10255 for vCore mongoClusters; instead use the exact connection string from the cluster portal/az output. For Entra ID auth follow cluster auth mode guidance if enabled. Use documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skills for recommended connection pooling and singleton client patterns.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older Cosmos connection string template and debugging options with modern Mongoose defaults; some options are legacy and SRV vs non-SRV patterns differ between the offerings.
confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding legacy options or replicaSet values may cause connection failures or compatibility warnings. Using outdated driver options may clutter code and cause confusion.
improvements: In the sample README show a single canonical connection example that reads DOCUMENTDB_URI and demonstrates recommended Mongoose 7+ connection (await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI)) and link to documentdb-driver skill for pooling and production config.

information_gaps.title: Default availability threshold
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for a configurable availability threshold but gives no default. Builders need a default value (e.g., 0.95). I searched the prompt and skills and found no recommended default for ATM availability thresholds.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset size recommendation
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires sample data but does not specify how many ATMs to seed for demos (20? 100?). The documentdb-local-deployment skill mentions sample-data scripts but not a recommended dataset size for this sample; the builder must decide.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when writing any IaC or CLI examples for vCore-managed MongoDB clusters.

Always read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime; do not hardcode ports or replicaSet values. For vCore clusters prefer the SRV connection string provided in the portal/az outputs and consult the cluster's connection-strings endpoint rather than assuming port 10255.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For local development use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (gateway exposes Mongo wire protocol on port 10260 with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256). If you cannot run the gateway, test against the live cluster given by DOCUMENTDB_URI.

If you plan to use multi-shard change streams, enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature in the cluster's Features (portal or CLI) before relying on cross-shard streaming; otherwise use collection.watch() for per-collection streams.
